meta.blurb: Something huge is sinking ships in the dark, and nobody knows what it is. Professor Aronnax sails out to hunt it. The monster is a steel ship, and its captain, Nemo, says no guest may ever leave.
meta.bible: Professor Pierre Aronnax: a French naturalist and the narrator, curious, careful and honest. Conseil: Aronnax's loyal servant, calm and fond of sorting living things into groups. Ned Land: a Canadian harpooner, strong, blunt and always dreaming of escape. Captain Nemo: the mysterious captain of the Nautilus; learned, proud, sad and angry with the world; his name means no one in Latin. Nautilus: Nemo's electric submarine, with a library, a museum, an organ and big glass windows. Commander Farragut: the captain of the American ship Abraham Lincoln. Abraham Lincoln: the warship sent to hunt the monster. La Pérouse: a French explorer whose ships were lost near Vanikoro in 1788. Vanikoro: a Pacific island where his ships were wrecked. Crespo: an island in the Pacific where Nemo hunts underwater. Torres Strait: the dangerous strait between New Guinea and Australia. New Guinea: the large island north of Australia. Ceylon: the island where pearls are fished. Indian Ocean, Red Sea, Pacific, Atlantic, Mediterranean, Antarctic: oceans and seas on the way. Suez: the narrow land between the Red Sea and the Mediterranean. Arabian Tunnel: the secret passage under it. Vigo Bay: a Spanish bay with sunken treasure. Atlantis: a lost city on the sea floor. Sargasso Sea: a sea covered with floating weed. Cape Horn: the southern tip of South America. Gulf Stream: the warm Atlantic current. Lofoten: the Norwegian islands where the story ends. Maelström: a dangerous whirlpool off Norway. New York: where Aronnax is when the story starts. Voice and tone: wonder and adventure, told by Aronnax, with calm scientific detail and a growing mystery about Nemo; keep every sea fact true; deaths are stated plainly with no gore.

B1B2: In 1866 ships all over the world report a giant sea animal, and some of them are badly damaged. Newspapers write about it every day, and nobody can say what it is.

Pierre Aronnax, a French professor, is visiting New York when he gets an invitation to join a ship that will hunt the monster. He agrees at once, and his faithful servant Conseil promises to come with him.
The captain of the ship, Commander Farragut, welcomes the professor. A tall Canadian called Ned Land, who is the best harpooner in the world, is on board, and he is ready to fight the monster.
The ship sails round South America and into the Pacific Ocean, and she searches for months without luck. Ned says that there is no monster, and the crew becomes tired and angry.
The ship chases the glowing shape through the night, and Ned throws his harpoon at it. It hits something hard and bounces off with a ring, and the monster swims away without a sound.

Late that night the monster hits the ship with great force, and Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land are thrown into the sea. They swim in the dark until they find a hard, smooth back to hold on to, and they see that it is made of steel.
Strange men pull the three castaways through a hatch and take them down into the steel ship. They are locked in a small, dark room, where there is a good meal waiting for them.
Then a tall man with dark eyes comes in and talks to them in perfect French. This is Captain Nemo, the master of the ship, and he says that they must live on his ship for ever.
Captain Nemo shows his guests around the Nautilus, and they are amazed. The ship has a huge library with twelve thousand books, and a large room full of fine paintings and shells.
In the salon, Aronnax sees cases full of shells, sea plants and the most beautiful pearls he has ever seen. Captain Nemo tells him that he found every one of them himself in the sea.
Captain Nemo explains that his ship runs on electricity, which he makes from the sea itself. It gives light, heat and power, and it lets the Nautilus travel under the water for months.
The Nautilus dives, and through the big windows the three men see fish and sea plants. Conseil is delighted, and he calls out the name of each fish, as a professor would.
Ned Land does not like being a prisoner, and he is always looking for a way to escape. Aronnax asks him to be patient while the Nautilus follows a warm current across the Pacific.
One day Nemo invites Aronnax to go hunting in the forests of Crespo Island, which are under the sea. He gives him a diving suit and an air gun that works by electricity.
Aronnax and Nemo leave the Nautilus and walk across the sandy sea floor. The weight of the water around them is great, and Aronnax feels as if he is flying in a dream.

After a long walk the two men reach a forest of tall plants that grow on the sea floor, and they stop to rest. Nemo points out plants and animals with simple signs, because it is not possible to speak.
Over the next weeks the Nautilus travels across the Pacific Ocean for thousands of leagues. Aronnax makes notes about every fish he sees, and Conseil sorts them into groups.
The Nautilus stops near Vanikoro, where the French explorer La Pérouse was lost with his ships in 1788. Aronnax sees the old wreck on the sea floor, and he thinks of the sailors who never came home.
The Nautilus enters the Torres Strait, a dangerous passage between New Guinea and Australia. It hits a reef, and the ship cannot move until the tide comes in.
Captain Nemo lets the three men go ashore in a small boat. They land on New Guinea, where they find coconuts and wild birds, and Ned is delighted to be on land again.
A crowd of local people chase the three men, and they race back to the boat. That night, the islanders climb onto the ship, but they get an electric shock from the rails and run away.
One of Nemo's men dies, and the crew buries him in a cemetery made of coral, deep under the sea. Aronnax sees how sad Nemo is, and he asks himself who these men are.
The Nautilus sails across the Indian Ocean to Ceylon, where people dive for pearls. Captain Nemo invites Aronnax to see the pearl beds, and he asks Ned and Conseil to come too.
Under the water Nemo shows Aronnax the oysters that make pearls. He points to a giant oyster that is more than a metre wide, and inside it is a huge pearl.
A shark swims towards a poor pearl diver, and Nemo steps in front of it with a knife. Ned Land kills the shark with a harpoon, and the diver is saved.
Afterwards Nemo gives the saved man a bag of pearls as a reward and then returns to the Nautilus. The professor thinks that a man who can be so generous may not be a bad man.
The Nautilus enters the Red Sea, and Nemo has news for Aronnax. He says that a secret passage lies under the land of Suez, the Arabian Tunnel, and the ship will use it to reach the Mediterranean.
The Nautilus enters the tunnel, and rushes through it. In a few minutes it comes out into the Mediterranean Sea, and Aronnax sees that Nemo has told the truth.

In the Mediterranean, Ned plans to escape in the small boat, because he thinks that they are close to land. But the Nautilus travels so fast that they are never near the coast, and a storm makes a boat impossible.
The Nautilus crosses the Mediterranean in two days, passing the Greek islands and the coast of Spain. Then it goes through the Strait of Gibraltar and enters the Atlantic Ocean.
In Vigo Bay, off the coast of Spain, some Spanish ships full of gold sank in 1702. Nemo and his crew bring the gold up from the sea bed, and he says it is for good use.
Nemo takes Aronnax to see the ruins of the lost city of Atlantis, lit by a volcano under the sea. Aronnax is amazed to see old walls and columns in the glow of the red light.
The Nautilus sails across the Sargasso Sea, a part of the Atlantic that is covered with floating weed. Nemo takes Aronnax to an underwater coal mine that he uses to make the ship's power.
The Nautilus finds a group of baleen whales that are being attacked by sperm whales. Nemo drives his ship among the attackers, and he saves the whales.
The Nautilus sails to the far south, where it is very cold. At the Antarctic ice barrier it cannot go on at the surface, so Nemo decides to dive below the ice.
At last the Nautilus comes to the South Pole, and Nemo plants a black flag with a letter N on it. He says that he takes the whole land for himself, and the three guests watch.
On the way back the ice closes around the Nautilus, and the ship is trapped under a roof of ice. The air in the ship gets bad, and everyone finds it hard to breathe.
Nemo orders the crew to break the ice, and they work in turn in diving suits for many days. At last the ship breaks free, and Aronnax gets fresh air again.
The Nautilus sails north past Cape Horn and along the coast of South America. It passes the mouth of the great Amazon River, and Aronnax sees fresh water pour into the sea.
Near the Gulf Stream, a group of giant squid, with long arms, attack the Nautilus. The crew goes on deck, and Ned and Nemo fight the squid with axes and harpoons.
One of the squid seizes a sailor and carries him away, and Nemo is full of sorrow. Aronnax sees tears on the captain's face, and he feels sorry for him.
Ned Land tells the professor that he has had enough of this ship. He says that they should try to escape the next time they are near land, and Aronnax agrees to think about it.
One day a warship appears and starts to fire on the Nautilus. Nemo's face is cold and hard, and he says that he is the law and that he is going to fight it.
Aronnax goes to his room, but he sees Nemo kneeling before a picture of a woman and children. Then he hears the Nautilus hit the ship, which sinks in a few minutes.
After the sinking, Nemo is silent and sad, and he does not speak to anyone. Aronnax thinks that he can no longer stay on a ship that is used for revenge, and he decides to leave.
Near Norway the three men get into the small boat. As they leave, they hear Nemo say a prayer, and they feel that something terrible is going to happen.
The boat falls into the Maelström, a huge whirlpool that spins round and round with a great roar. Aronnax hits his head hard, and everything turns dark.
When Aronnax wakes, he is in a fisherman's hut on the Lofoten Islands in Norway. Ned and Conseil are safe, and they are kind to the fishermen who saved them.
Aronnax goes home to France and writes down the story of his journey under the sea. He does not know if the Nautilus escaped the Maelström, or if Nemo is still alive.
Aronnax finishes by saying that he hopes Nemo has found peace and that his hatred has gone. He wishes that the Nautilus is still sailing, and that the sea still shelters its captain.
C1C2: In the year 1866 sailors on many oceans report a gigantic creature that moves faster than any whale and shines at night with a strange light, and several ships come home with deep holes in their sides. The newspapers of Europe and America are full of the mystery, and every learned man seems to have his own opinion. Nobody can say for certain what the monster is, but everybody agrees that it must be found.

Professor Aronnax, a respected French naturalist who happens to be in New York at the time, is invited by the American government to join the hunt for the monster as an expert. He accepts with a clear mind and a feeling of adventure, and his devoted servant Conseil, who has followed him everywhere for years, decides to come as well. They hurry together to the harbour, where a fast and well-armed ship is already waiting to carry them out to sea.

The Abraham Lincoln is a fast and well-armed ship under Commander Farragut, and her crew includes the finest harpooner in the world, a tall and stubborn Canadian called Ned Land. Ned does not believe in sea monsters, but he loves a hunt, and he and the professor soon become friends. The ship leaves New York harbour with the crew cheering and the whole country watching.

For many weeks the Abraham Lincoln follows every rumour from Cape Horn up into the Pacific Ocean, but the great sea gives up no monster, and the crew's spirits sink. Ned Land begins to say aloud that the whole tale is nonsense, and Commander Farragut promises the sailors that they will turn home within three days. Then, on the very last night, a long glow appears in the dark water.

Commander Farragut orders full speed in pursuit of the glowing shape, and Ned Land climbs to the front of the ship with his harpoon ready. When he finally throws it, the point strikes with a dull metallic ring and falls away, and the thing slides off into the dark at a speed no animal could match. Aronnax begins to wonder whether they are hunting a creature of flesh at all.

Just before midnight the creature turns and strikes the ship at her side, and in the confusion Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land are hurled overboard and into the waves. The Abraham Lincoln drifts away into the dark, and the three men, half drowned, swim to the one thing in sight, a long, dark island of metal that floats on the water. It is no sea animal, they realise with a shock, but a ship of steel, and some unknown person must have built it.

After many hours clinging to the steel hull, the three castaways are seized by a group of silent men and lowered into the dark interior of the vessel. There they are locked in a bare cell, with no light and no explanation, until at last a lamp is lit and food is brought for them. Aronnax, hungry and confused, understands that they have found the monster and that they have been captured by it.

At last the door opens, and a tall man with a pale face and piercing dark eyes enters and speaks to them in fluent French. He introduces himself as Captain Nemo, master of the ship, and he tells them calmly that he has left the land for ever and cannot allow anyone who has seen his secret to leave. The three men are not prisoners, he says, but guests who must remain with him until the end of their days.

Captain Nemo leads the three men through the ship, which he calls the Nautilus, and shows them a library that holds twelve thousand books in many languages. Beyond it lies a salon like a museum, filled with rare shells, pearls, paintings and statues, and even a great organ that Nemo plays at night. Aronnax, a lover of science, cannot help admiring the sheer beauty of it all.

In the great salon the cases of glass hold the treasures of every ocean, from delicate shells to coral and from sea plants to pearls larger than any he has ever seen. Nemo explains, with quiet pride, that he gathered each treasure with his own hands, and that the sea has given him everything he needs. Aronnax realises that he has met a man of rare learning, and perhaps of rare sorrow.

Captain Nemo shows Aronnax the engine room and explains that everything on the Nautilus, from the lamps to the engine, runs on electricity that he draws from the sea. It supplies the light, the heat and the power, and it allows the ship to cross whole oceans beneath the waves without ever needing to touch land. The sea, says Nemo, belongs to no king, and on its surface he has no rulers, which is why he loves it.

When the Nautilus sinks below the waves, the big windows of the salon open like the eyes of a dream, and a garden of fish, plants and corals sweeps past in the lamp light. Conseil, who loves to arrange every living creature in its class and family, names each one with great joy, and Aronnax can hardly look away. For the first time, the professor feels that he is seeing the sea as it truly is.

Ned Land, who hates being shut in, spends every day plotting some way to get free, and he is deeply angry at Captain Nemo for taking away his freedom. Aronnax urges patience, for the Nautilus is carrying them across the Pacific along a great warm river called the Black Current, and he is eager to see all the wonders of the deep. Conseil, as always, is content simply to watch and to learn, and he writes down the names of the wonders that pass the window.

One morning Captain Nemo offers Aronnax a very unusual invitation: to join him on a hunt in the underwater forests that surround Crespo Island. Aronnax is given a heavy diving suit with a tank of air on his back, and a special gun that fires small electric bullets. Conseil and Ned Land, to their great regret, are told to wait on board, and they watch their friend vanish through the hatch.

Aronnax and Nemo step out of the ship onto the sandy floor of the sea, and the water presses on their suits like a heavy hand, while sunlight filters down in green beams from far above. They walk for hours across plains of white sand, past strange rocks and shells, with the Nautilus fading behind them in the blue. Aronnax feels as though he has become a visitor to another world, one that no other man of his time has ever seen.

Beyond the plains the two men reach a dense forest of tall sea plants that sway in the current like trees in a gentle wind, and they rest among them in the green light. Captain Nemo points out each plant and animal with simple gestures, for no word can be heard through their helmets, and Aronnax understands that the sea is his teacher's real home. When the hunt is over, they carry their game back across the sand to the Nautilus, tired but filled with wonder at what they have seen.

Over the following weeks the Nautilus covers some four thousand leagues across the Pacific, passing coral reefs and island groups, and Aronnax fills his notebook with every new fish and plant that he sees. Conseil, never tired of learning, sorts them into groups with great pleasure, and even Ned Land cannot resist being impressed. Yet the captain himself stays distant and polite, and he keeps his thoughts to himself, so that Aronnax can only guess at his secrets.

The Nautilus reaches the island of Vanikoro, where, in 1788, the French explorer La Pérouse lost both of his ships, and the fate of his crew remained a mystery for many years. Through the great windows Aronnax sees the old wreckage resting on the sea bed, and he thinks of the brave men who sailed into the unknown and never came home. Captain Nemo watches in silence, and seems to know more than he is willing to say.

The Nautilus enters the Torres Strait, a narrow and dangerous passage between New Guinea and Australia, where hidden rocks and reefs make travel difficult. In the darkness the ship runs aground, and Captain Nemo calmly says that she will float again in a few days, when the tide has risen. For Ned Land the island on the horizon looks like a gift from heaven.

Nemo gives them permission to go ashore in the ship's small boat, and they land on the green coast of New Guinea, where Ned eagerly hunts birds and Conseil gathers coconuts and other fruit. For the first time in months they walk on firm ground under real trees, and they forget the sea for an afternoon. Then Conseil points out a group of local people watching them from the trees.

When the islanders come out of the forest with weapons in their hands, the three friends retreat to the boat and row hard for the Nautilus. Next morning hundreds of canoes surround the ship, and many climb on to the deck, but the iron rails carry an electric current, and one touch is enough to send each man leaping back. By the afternoon the tide has risen, and the Nautilus floats free of the reef and glides safely out of the dangerous strait.

After an accident on board, one of Captain Nemo's sailors dies, and the crew carries the body in silence to a cemetery of living coral on the sea floor. Aronnax, watching the burial, sees the grief on Nemo's face and wonders what bond could unite these men, and what brought them to give up the land forever. He does not dare ask, for he sees that the captain wishes to be alone.

Crossing the Indian Ocean, the Nautilus arrives off Ceylon, the island famous for its pearl fisheries, and Captain Nemo offers to take Aronnax to the oyster beds on the sea floor. He tells him that pearl fishing is an ancient trade, and he adds, with a half smile, that he will not need to hire any divers. Ned Land and Conseil are invited to join them, and Ned, who has fished all his life, can hardly hide his curiosity.

At the bottom of the sea Nemo leads Aronnax among the oyster beds, and shows him a gigantic shell, more than a metre across, that has a pearl as large as a coconut. He tells the professor that such a pearl would be worth a fortune, but he has no wish to sell it, and he watches over it as a guardian. Aronnax admires the gift but cannot help wondering why this strange man is so wealthy.

A pearl diver appears above them on the sea bed, just as a huge shark turns to attack him, and Captain Nemo throws himself in the creature's path with a knife in his hand. The shark's jaws are open and the knife is nearly lost, but Ned Land darts forward with his harpoon, and the beast dies at last. The man is pulled alive to the surface, thanks to the quick courage of the captain and the harpooner who fought side by side.

Back on the surface, Nemo puts into the rescued man's hands a purse of pearls, as if the whole fortune meant nothing to him, and he returns silently to the ship. Aronnax, who has seen so much that is strange and hard about the captain, is surprised and moved by this act, and he thinks that a heart so kind cannot be altogether closed. Nemo says that he hates mankind, and yet, as Aronnax notes with wonder, he has just risked his own life to save a stranger.

Sailing north through the Red Sea, the Nautilus approaches the narrow land of Suez, where no ship can pass without a canal, and Captain Nemo reveals to Aronnax that there is a secret way under the earth. He calls it the Arabian Tunnel, and says that he has been using it for years, and that he will guide his ship through it that very night. Aronnax, who has no idea that such a thing is possible, can hardly believe his ears and waits for the night with great impatience.

At dusk the Nautilus dives into the narrow opening and races through the passage, with the water boiling in its wake and the lamps trembling on the walls. Within minutes the ship comes out into the open water of the Mediterranean, and Aronnax understands that a captain who can move so freely between two seas is truly master of the oceans. He feels a strange mixture of admiration, fear and wonder, and he knows that he will never forget this journey as long as he lives.

Ned Land, convinced that the Mediterranean will give him his chance, plans to escape in the ship's small boat and urges his two friends to join him. But the Nautilus travels so swiftly, and keeps so far from shore, that there is never a moment when the plan could work, and a heavy storm makes the little boat useless anyway. Ned grinds his teeth in anger, but he knows that he must wait for a better chance, and he tells his friends that it will surely come.

Passing the Greek islands, Aronnax thinks of the old stories of gods and heroes, and he regrets that he can only glimpse the sea around them through a window. In only two days the Nautilus crosses the whole of the Mediterranean, slips through the Strait of Gibraltar, and enters the open Atlantic Ocean, which Nemo greets as an old friend. The professor finds that his wonder at the captain's speed never fades, and he asks himself how one man could have built such a ship alone.

In Vigo Bay, on the coast of Spain, a fleet of Spanish treasure ships was sunk in a great sea battle in 1702, and much of its gold is thought to lie there still. Captain Nemo and his men walk across the sea bed, filling chests with the lost treasure, and he tells Aronnax calmly that the gold has no owner now, and that he knows how best to use it. The professor sees how rich a man of the sea can be, and he wonders what kind of life lies behind such quiet and secret power.

At night Captain Nemo takes Aronnax across a dark plain on the Atlantic sea bed, where the glow of a distant volcano lights up the broken walls, columns and arches of a great, sunken city. Nemo tells him that this is Atlantis, which the ancients wrote about, and Aronnax, with his head full of old stories, stands amazed before a world that the sea has swallowed up. He wishes that he could stay for ever in that silent place, and he is sorry when the captain gives the sign to return to the ship.

Leaving the ruins, the Nautilus passes through the Sargasso Sea, where floating weed covers the water for hundreds of miles and the ship has to move carefully to avoid being tangled. Nemo takes Aronnax to a coal mine under the sea, and explains that the sodium he uses for power can be made from the sea itself and, if necessary, from the coal. The professor is quietly amazed by the cleverness of the whole arrangement, and he sees that Captain Nemo has solved every problem that the sea can offer.

South of the Azores, Aronnax sees a herd of baleen whales being hunted by a pack of fierce sperm whales, and Captain Nemo, who hates cruelty to any sea creature, drives the Nautilus straight into the fight. Using the ship's steel ram, he scatters the attackers, and Ned Land, who loves a good hunt, cheers with all his might. The whales are saved, and Aronnax understands that the captain's care for the sea is real.

Sailing south, the Nautilus enters the cold seas near the Antarctic, where great icebergs drift across the water and the horizon is white. When the ship reaches the great ice barrier, it cannot travel on the surface any further, and Captain Nemo, with a calm smile, announces that he will go beneath the ice. Ned Land looks at the white wall with a shiver, for he has never felt such cold.

The Nautilus reaches the land at the bottom of the world, and Captain Nemo, standing in the freezing wind, measures the sun to find the exact point of the South Pole. He plants a black flag marked with a gold letter N and announces that he takes possession of this land, which no other man has seen, and the three prisoners can only watch in silence. It is, Aronnax thinks, the proudest moment of the captain's strange life, though he cannot tell whether it fills Nemo with joy or with sorrow.

When the Nautilus tries to leave, a huge iceberg turns over and closes the water around the ship, so that it is trapped in a small icy tunnel with no way out. Slowly the air grows stale, and the men begin to gasp, and Aronnax lies on the floor of the salon, feeling that this may be the end. Even Nemo's quiet face has lost its calm, and for the first time Aronnax sees that the captain himself may not know how to escape.

Captain Nemo sets his whole crew to work, and in diving suits they cut away the ice around the ship in turn, day and night, while the water around them freezes again almost as fast as they can break it. At last the Nautilus, driven by its own power and by the hot water that Nemo pours on the ice, breaks through to the open sea, and every man drinks in the fresh air. Aronnax, who a day before thought that he would never see the sun again, has never in his life been so glad simply to breathe.

After the ice, the Nautilus heads north along the shore of South America, rounds Cape Horn and continues until it reaches the mouth of the mighty Amazon River. Aronnax gazes at the fresh water that pours into the Atlantic and spreads over the salt sea, and he thinks of all the wonders he has seen on this voyage. Yet he cannot forget for a moment that he is still a prisoner, and that every wonder is a part of a voyage he did not choose.

Off the coast of North America, enormous squid, each with arms many metres long, rise from the deep and surround the Nautilus, and Captain Nemo orders his crew onto the deck to fight them with axes. Ned Land, never one to run from a battle, stands at his captain's side and strikes at the arms with his harpoon. Aronnax watches from the hatch, and he has never seen anything so terrible and so strange.

In the heat of the struggle, one of the giant creatures seizes a crewman and carries him off, and no one can reach him in time. Captain Nemo, who has shown no weakness until now, breaks down and weeps, and Aronnax sees that the man he has called a monster can feel as much sorrow as anyone. For days after the battle, the captain does not leave his room, and the whole ship seems to hold its breath until he is ready to appear.

When Nemo's grief has passed, Ned Land tells Aronnax that he cannot wait any longer and that the first chance they get, they must run. Aronnax, who has begun to understand the captain's sadness, hesitates, for he loves the sea and the knowledge it brings, but he also longs for home and family. Finally he promises Ned that he will join him when the moment comes, though he feels that he is promising to leave something precious behind.

A warship appears on the horizon and opens fire on the Nautilus, and Captain Nemo's calm face hardens into a mask of hatred. He tells Aronnax that he is the law and the judge in this place, and that the ship before him belongs to a country that has done him a great wrong. Aronnax, still doubtful, is ordered to go to his room with Ned and Conseil.

Locked in the corridor, Aronnax sees through the half-open door of the captain's room that Nemo is kneeling before the portrait of a woman and two young children, with his hands clasped. A moment later he feels a great shock, as the Nautilus drives her steel ram into the warship, and the vessel sinks beneath the waves. Aronnax is horrified, for he wants no part in such a revenge, and he understands at last why Nemo's heart is so heavy with hatred and grief.

In the days after the battle, Captain Nemo is a changed man, gloomy and silent, and the Nautilus drifts north without any plan. Aronnax feels pity for him, but he cannot forgive what he has seen, and he knows that if they stay, the voyage will end badly. He tells Ned and Conseil that they must flee as soon as the ship nears land.

Off the coast of Norway the three men creep to the boat in the dark, and they are almost free when Aronnax hears the crew murmuring a prayer, and then a cry of despair from Captain Nemo. They feel the Nautilus shudder as it is dragged towards the great whirlpool of the Maelström, and they cast off in a panic. Behind them the great ship is lost to sight in the whirling water, and the three men can only pray that they too will survive.

The little boat is caught in the whirling water of the Maelström, which spins around and around with a deafening roar, and Aronnax is thrown against the side and loses consciousness. He does not know what happens to the Nautilus, and for a few moments the whole world is nothing but water, noise and cold. Then the boat is flung clear of the whirlpool by some lucky chance, and Aronnax knows nothing more of what happens that night.

Aronnax opens his eyes and finds himself in a fisherman's hut on the Lofoten Islands, off the coast of Norway, with Ned and Conseil safe beside him. The boat has been thrown free of the Maelström by some miracle, and the fishermen who found them have been kindly. They are free, and Aronnax can hardly believe that the whole adventure is over.

Back in France, Aronnax writes down every detail of his strange journey, so that the world may know that the sea is far richer than anyone has dreamed. He does not know whether the Nautilus survived the Maelström, or where Captain Nemo is now, but he hopes that the captain still lives. Nobody, he says, has ever seen as much of the sea as he has, in some twenty thousand leagues beneath its waves.

Aronnax closes his account with a wish that Captain Nemo has found peace at last, and that the hatred which made him a wanderer has finally faded from his heart. He hopes that the Nautilus is still crossing the oceans, with its great windows full of marvels, and that the sea, the only home Nemo ever loved, still shelters him. The learned world will decide whether his story is true, but he, Pierre Aronnax, knows that it is.
